The Cursor SDK launches agents with the same harness, runtime and models. env.type cloud uses Cursor-hosted VMs; pool and machine route to the customer's own workers, and pools do not move the agent loop out of Cursor's cloud. A Security Reviewer triggered by a PR event runs on Cursor-managed hosting. openAsCursorGithubApp applies only if autoCreatePr is true.

order_note.quote: Team Rules work alongside other rule types and take precedence.
order_note.text: Team rules work alongside other rule types and take precedence over them.

house-rules.plain: Cloud agents read the project's instruction file, and the CLI and editor load project rules on their own. Rules can be scoped to file patterns and can include other files. User rules and project rules both go into the prompt, and team rules take precedence.
house-rules.technical: Cloud agents read AGENTS.md; rules in .cursor/rules load automatically; Bugbot uses .cursor/BUGBOT.md. Rules are .mdc files scoped by path patterns (Apply to Specific Files, e.g. *.tsx); @filename.ts includes a file. User rules are set in Cursor Settings. Cursor project rules (*.mdc) do not apply to Bugbot runs; use .cursor/BUGBOT.md or rules configured in Automations.

loop.plain: The agent calls a tool, reads the result and decides its next step. The documentation says there is no limit on the number of tool calls in a task. A stop hook can send a follow-up message to keep it going, with a default limit of 5.
loop.technical: A stop hook is called when the agent loop ends and can optionally auto-submit a follow-up user message. There is no limit on the number of tool calls Agent can make during a task. Stop-hook auto follow-ups have a default limit of 5 per script, configurable via loop_limit; null removes the cap. The same limit applies to subagentStop follow-ups.

memory-sessions.plain: It can keep notes between runs of an automation and save a learned rule from a pull request comment. You can continue, fork, rename and list past chats, and send a chat to a cloud agent, but uncommitted local changes do not go with it.
memory-sessions.technical: Automation memories persist as named entries (MEMORIES.md by default); @cursor remember [fact] on a PR saves a Bugbot learned rule. --continue (alias for --resume=-1); --resume [thread id]; /fork; /rename <name>; agent ls. Prepending & to a CLI message pushes the chat to a Cloud Agent; 'Move to Cloud' does not snapshot local uncommitted changes. Hooks get transcript_path (null if transcripts disabled).

order_note.quote: resolves the user default model, then the team default, then a system default
order_note.text: For the cloud agent interface, an omitted model choice falls back from the user default to the team default to a system default.

model-effort.plain: You choose the model from a picker in chat or a command in the command line, and can set a default in settings. Effort levels depend on the model, and Composer has none. You can add your own key for a supported provider. The documentation does not mention shared model selection.
model-effort.technical: Model picker dropdown; default in Cursor Settings > Models; CLI /model. Cloud Agent API resolves the user default model, then the team default, then a system default. Effort is per model: Grok 4.5 high (default), medium, low; Grok 4.6 adds xhigh. Set with model.params, ModelSelection.params or square-bracket id=value options. On Cursor Start, Grok 4.5 is fixed at medium. US data residency is not supported for BYOK.

org-oversight.plain: Single sign-on is listed among team features, and a policy controls which team IDs can log in. Enterprise customers can enroll in US-only data residency, and a few models fall outside the data retention agreements. Admins are advised to review audit logs.
org-oversight.technical: SAML/OIDC SSO is listed among Teams features; the AllowedTeamId policy logs out users with unauthorized team IDs; SCIM directory groups are used for team-level spend and policy. Enterprise can enroll in US-only data residency; CMEK for Cloud Agent data. A few models require data retention with the provider and fall outside these agreements. Audit logs: review periodically and stream to a SIEM.

order_note.quote: A team-defined global Auto-review configuration takes priority
order_note.text: A team-defined global automatic-review setting takes priority, and Cursor ignores user-level and project-level files.

org-policy.plain: Companies can deploy Cursor with enforced policies through device management, and team hooks sync from a dashboard. Locking network access and limiting models or MCP servers are Enterprise features, and a team review setting takes priority over personal ones.
org-policy.technical: MDM enforces policies (allowed team IDs, extensions); ~/.cursor/permissions.json can be distributed through MDM for the per-user MCP auto-run allowlist. Team hooks are set in the web dashboard (Enterprise for enterprise-managed hooks). Lock Network Access Policy and the MCP allowlist are Enterprise; model control needs contacting sales, and non-ZDR models need admin approval.

order_note.quote: after a connection is approved, each tool call still needs individual approval before running
order_note.text: A connection is approved first; after that each tool call still needs its own approval.

outside-tools.plain: It connects outside tools through MCP in the editor, the command line and cloud agents. Each connection needs approval, and each tool call needs approval unless pre-approved. The documentation gives conflicting answers on whether cloud agents accept one older connection style.
outside-tools.technical: Servers are defined in project or user .cursor/mcp.json (command and args; headers or OAuth; env for stdio); agent mcp login <identifier>. Cloud agents: HTTP or stdio; inline definitions (maximum 50). Docs say SSE and mcp-remote are not supported for cloud-agent custom servers, yet the Python SDK type accepts 'http' or 'sse'. Allowlist: configure in the team dashboard (Enterprise only). mcpAllowlist uses server:tool.

order_note.quote: when set, it overrides the in-app terminal allowlist
order_note.text: A terminal allow list, when set, overrides the in-app terminal allow list.

permission-check.plain: Rules decide what runs without a prompt, by tool, file pattern or command, and an automatic reviewer can check calls outside the sandbox. Allow lists are a convenience, not a security guarantee, and terminal commands can still read ignored files.
permission-check.technical: permissions.allow, permissions.deny and --force control what runs without prompts; mcpAllowlist; terminalAllowlist entries are matched against the full command string. Read permissions support glob patterns; .cursorignore blocks files from Agent, codebase search and @ mentions. Terminal commands and MCP tools run outside Cursor's file access controls. Allowlists and autoRun are best-effort.

plan-and-ask.plain: Plan mode researches the code, asks clarifying questions and writes a plan you can edit before building starts. File editing is listed as allowed after you approve the plan. A status line and a context ring show progress and how full the window is.
plan-and-ask.technical: Plan Mode researches the codebase, asks clarifying questions and generates a reviewable plan; enter via Shift+Tab, /plan, --plan or --mode=plan. Over ACP, cursor/create_plan blocks until the client accepts or rejects. File editing is listed as 'Yes (after you approve the plan)'; Plan mode is not labelled read-only. /statusline configures the CLI status line; the context ring opens a breakdown tray.

order_note.quote: its value overrides the corresponding Cursor setting on users' devices
order_note.text: When a policy comes from device management, its value overrides the matching Cursor setting on the user's device.

safety-posture.plain: Terminal commands need approval by default. Run modes range from an allow list to an automatic reviewer, and a run-everything mode skips prompts. Plan, ask, debug and design modes exist. The new-folder trust question is off by default; a device policy overrides matching settings.
safety-posture.technical: Terminal commands need approval by default. CLI approvalMode: allowlist, auto-review or unrestricted; -f/--force; --yolo; /run-everything [on|off|status] (alias /auto-run). --mode takes plan or ask (agent default). Workspace trust is disabled by default and restricted mode breaks AI features; docs differ on whether --trust works in headless mode only or in interactive sessions too.

send-retry.plain: At the usage limit you see a notice and can switch on pay-as-you-go or upgrade. Auto uses a router that sends simple requests to fast models and complex work to the most capable ones. The documentation advises backing off with growing delays when rate limited.
send-retry.technical: Cursor Router is the routing behind Auto; on Teams and Enterprise it picks the model for each Auto request based on your optimization mode. A Fable request that trips a security guardrail is routed to Claude Opus. One endpoint is rate limited to 300 requests per minute and 6000 per hour; back off with exponential delay (SDK reports isRetryable: true for transient cases).

shrink-context.plain: When the window nears full, Cursor summarises older parts of the conversation to make room, and you can do it by hand with a command. A hook runs before compaction but cannot block or change it.
shrink-context.technical: Cursor compresses older conversation into a summary when the context window gets close to full. The preCompact hook is observational; it cannot block or modify compaction. /summarize frees up space; /compress is an alias; /compact and /compress remain as aliases that execute directly.

skills-commands.plain: Skills are folders of instructions the agent can pick when a task fits, or you can run one by typing a slash and its name. Commands are saved prompts kept at team, project or user level. The documentation does not mention per-skill tool or model overrides.
skills-commands.technical: Skills are SKILL.md files in a directory under skills/; .cursor/skills/ is walked recursively; descriptions are injected, references/ and scripts/ load on demand. Invoke with / or @. Commands live in .cursor/commands (.md, .mdc, .markdown, .txt). Built-ins: /model [filter], /in-cloud, /agent-review, /side or /btw. disable-model-invocation: true makes a skill act like a slash command.

subagents.plain: Helper agents are set up as text files with their own model, tools and read-only choice, and several can run at once in their own context. The main agent and its direct helpers can start helpers; one started by another helper cannot start more.
subagents.technical: Custom subagents: markdown in .cursor/agents/; model defaults to inherit; readonly: true (default false). Since Cursor 2.5 subagents can launch child subagents; a subagent launched by another subagent can't launch further ones. Built-ins: Explore, Bash, Browser. Maximum 20 custom subagents per Cloud Agent API run; one active run per agent (409 agent_busy); self-hosted up to 200 workers per user, 1000 per team.

surface.plain: You can reach Cursor from a terminal, from JetBrains editors, from its own editor and agents window, from a browser, from a script or code library, and from chat and code-hosting tools such as Slack, Teams and GitHub comments.
surface.technical: Cursor CLI with no command starts interactive agent mode; -p/--print is non-interactive, with --output-format json, stream-json or text. agent acp runs the CLI as an ACP server over stdio (JetBrains IDEs). Cloud Agents run at cursor.com/agents; Agent.create() takes local or cloud. @cursor works in Slack, GitHub, Bitbucket and Microsoft Teams.

thinking.plain: Which thinking options exist depends on the model. The command line can show the model's thinking blocks, and the cloud agent run stream sends thinking text. The documentation says thinking events are suppressed in print mode.
thinking.technical: Options depend on the model; each model entry in the API response lists accepted id+params combinations. Grok 4.6: xhigh, high (default), medium, low; Muse Spark 1.3: six levels, minimal to max, high default; Grok 4.5: high (default), medium, low. display.showThinkingBlocks renders thinking blocks. thinking events are suppressed in print mode, but the cloud-agent run stream emits them.

unattended.plain: Automations run cloud agents in the background on a schedule or when events arrive from tools such as GitHub, Slack and Linear. Cloud agents work in full development environments and keep going when your device disconnects. You can take over the remote desktop and hand it back.
unattended.technical: Automations run cloud agents on a schedule or on events from GitHub, GitLab, Slack, webhooks, Linear. Commenting @cursor on a GitHub PR or issue starts an agent. Subagent is_background: true (default false). /loop skill; timer subscriptions are a one-off reminder or a recurring cron schedule. /in-cloud hands a task to a cloud subagent on its own VM and branch.

undo-point.plain: Restoring a checkpoint on an earlier message rolls back the files the agent changed after that point, but the conversation keeps its messages. The command line can jump back to a previous message, and forking a chat from an earlier message shortens the conversation.
undo-point.technical: Restore Checkpoint on a previous message rolls back all changes Agent made after that point; it reverts files only and does not remove messages from the conversation. In the CLI, /rewind jumps back to a previous message, and the rewind config field enables it. To shorten the conversation, fork the chat from an earlier message.

updates.plain: The command line tries to update itself by default, and there are Stable and Early Access channels. A device policy can switch updates off. Changelog pages list new features and fixes, and the documentation gives some deprecations as examples.
updates.technical: Channels: Stable (default) and Early Access; CLI config field channel. CLI tries to auto-update by default; /update; UpdateMode MDM policy (update.mode) set to 'none' disables updates. agent --version; /about. SDK changelog covers @cursor/sdk on npm and cursor-sdk on PyPI. Examples: sdk.v1 changes additively; Ask Every Time is deprecated in 3.5; --pool-name is a deprecated alias for --pool <name>.

workspace.plain: The command line can run the agent in a new Git worktree instead of your current checkout, and agents started that way from the agents window get a separate checkout. Helper agents share the parent's checkout by default. Worktrees are disabled for multi-root workspaces.
workspace.technical: -w/--worktree [name] runs the CLI agent in a new Git worktree under ~/.cursor/worktrees/<reponame>/<name>. Agents started in a worktree from the Agents Window get a separate checkout. Subagents share the parent's checkout by default; on request each runs in its own copy. Features that rely on a single git root, like worktrees, are disabled for multi-root workspaces.

wrap-up.plain: A spending dashboard shows the cost of requests, and you can fetch billed token use for an agent. You are asked to set a spend limit when you first use cloud agents. Usage metrics can stream to monitoring tools for Enterprise, and a command shows the debug log location.
wrap-up.technical: Spending dashboard shows request-level cost and pool details; getUsage fetches billed token usage and dollar cost. Spend limit is requested on first use of Cloud Agents; groups have Spend Limit Overrides. OpenTelemetry Export (OTLP) is Enterprise only; on by default except conversation_content. /logs shows the debug log path; --data-dir <path> sets the base directory on the worker.

assemble-prompt.plain: You can pull in file contents with an at-sign reference, add extra directories to the workspace, and exclude files through ignore rules. The documentation does not mention the size of the context window.
assemble-prompt.technical: @ in a prompt triggers read_many_files, which reads and concatenates content from multiple files. --include-directories adds directories (comma-separated or multiple flags). A setting makes searches respect .gitignore files; .geminiignore files provide exclusion patterns. The documentation does not mention the context window size.

built-in-tools.plain: It gives the model tools to search and read files, edit them, run shell commands, which need manual confirmation, and search or fetch from the web. A setting can restrict the set of built-in tools, and a command lists the ones available.
built-in-tools.technical: grep_search (legacy alias search_file_content); glob, list_directory, read_many_files; run_shell_command runs shell commands, supports interactive sessions and background processes, requires manual confirmation (node-pty). google_web_search; web_fetch validates requests against private and reserved IP ranges and in Plan Mode requires explicit user confirmation. /tools lists available tools.

order_note.quote: it overrides the blockGitExtensions setting
order_note.text: The allowed-extensions list overrides the setting that blocks extensions from Git.

extend-share.plain: Extensions bundle prompts, tool connections, custom commands, themes and helpers, and install from a repository address or local path. Management commands take effect after a restart. The gallery route covers public extensions, which it indexes automatically.
extend-share.technical: gemini-extension.json manifest; loads from <home>/.gemini/extensions; gemini extensions install <source> (Git URL or local path); --auto-update. HEAD commit is treated as latest; commands take effect after you restart the CLI session. The gallery route covers public extensions: it automatically indexes public extensions (topic gemini-cli-extension). security.allowedExtensions, --consent, admin setting.

fence.plain: A sandbox can be switched on and is documented as off by default. On Mac, a profile confines writes to the project folder. The sandbox page describes network as allowed, while a network access setting is documented with a default of off, so the two differ.
fence.technical: --sandbox (-s), default false; a macOS Seatbelt profile confines writes to the project folder; tools.sandboxAllowedPaths (default []); tools.sandboxNetworkAccess (default false), while the sandbox page describes writes to the project directory with broad file reads and network allowed. v0.35.0 added Linux bubblewrap/seccomp. On a permission failure a Request step shows a modal dialog.

hooks.plain: Hooks run your own scripts at set moments, such as before a model request. For now just command-type hooks are supported, non-text message parts are filtered out, and one event does not support some blocking controls. Project hooks start untrusted.
hooks.technical: Events include BeforeModel, BeforeToolSelection, AfterAgent. Handler type: currently only 'command'. BeforeModel input has llm_request (model, messages, config); non-text parts are filtered out. Exit Code 2 aborts the turn and skips the LLM call. BeforeToolSelection does not support decision, continue. hooksConfig.enabled (default true); project hooks untrusted by default.

host-platform.plain: It runs on Mac, Windows and Ubuntu with a recent Node runtime. Google AI Pro or Ultra gives higher limits shared with agent mode in the IDE, while Workspace plans do not cover its API usage. The documentation does not mention shared servers or a shared runtime.
host-platform.technical: macOS 15+, Windows 11 24H2+, Ubuntu 20.04+; Node.js 20.0.0+; Bash, Zsh, or PowerShell. Google AI Pro or Ultra: higher limits shared across Gemini CLI and IDE agent mode; Gemini for workspace plans do not apply to the API usage; organization tiers apply on Workspace sign-in. Not mentioned: shared execution infrastructure, shared agent runtime, delegates to, distinct harness features.

order_note.quote: starting from the current working directory and then in each parent directory up to a stop point
order_note.text: The search starts in the current folder and moves up through the parent folders to a stop point.

house-rules.plain: It reads instruction files from your home folder and project, searching from the current folder upward and joining what it finds. Files can import other files, and a file in a subfolder holds rules for that folder. It also scans a folder when a tool touches it.
house-rules.technical: Default context file name GEMINI.md (a setting names others); global ~/.gemini/GEMINI.md, project-root ./GEMINI.md, ./src/GEMINI.md for the src folder. Found from the current working directory up through parent directories to a stop point and concatenated. @path/to/file.md imports, nested allowed. When a tool accesses a file or directory, the CLI scans for GEMINI.md files there.

loop.plain: The core returns tool results to the model for further processing. Turn limits cap a session, a helper's turns, and tool calls per task. Detection of infinite loops can be turned off, and a particular output value can stop the loop at once.
loop.technical: A continue field set to false kills the entire agent loop immediately; automatic infinite-loop detection can be disabled via a setting. model.maxSessionTurns caps turns (-1 means unlimited); subagent max_turns defaults to 30; maxActionsPerTask caps tool calls per task; exit code 53 means the session turn maximum was reached (non-interactive mode).

memory-sessions.plain: It keeps durable notes, and an experimental feature drafts new ones from past sessions for you to approve. You can resume, branch and list earlier sessions, saved as local transcripts. For handoff, the documentation describes exporting sessions to files.
memory-sessions.technical: Auto Memory is experimental: patches are held for review in /memory inbox until approved. /memory reload scans include directories when context.loadMemoryFromIncludeDirectories is true; when false, just the current directory is used. --resume (-r) takes latest or an index; /resume save forks; --list-sessions; history in ~/.gemini. Handoff is documented as the ability to export sessions to files.

model-effort.plain: You pick the model in a dialog or at launch, and the default is automatic. A Gemini API key is an alternative to a Google sign-in, but an unpaid key is capped at 250 requests a day on the Flash model. The documentation does not mention effort levels or shared model choice.
model-effort.technical: /model dialog; --model (-m) default auto; model.name default undefined. Auto (Gemini 3) picks gemini-3-pro-preview or gemini-3-flash-preview. Unpaid Gemini API key: 250 maximum model requests / user / day, Flash model. thinkingConfig sits in generateContentConfig. Not mentioned: effort values, shared model selection.

org-oversight.plain: Sign-in is with a Google account for Gemini Code Assist, and Workspace accounts get organization tiers. Old session data is cleaned up automatically by default. A telemetry and auditing section covers configuring the CLI for monitoring.
org-oversight.technical: security.auth.enforcedType in system-level settings.json sets the required auth type. Organization tiers apply on Google Workspace sign-in. Old session data is cleaned up automatically by default; --delete on exit deletes the session; set logPrompts to false in an enterprise setting. Telemetry and auditing section: configure Gemini CLI for auditing and monitoring.

order_note.quote: Admin policies always override User, Workspace, and Default policies.
order_note.text: Admin policies win over user, workspace and default policies.

org-policy.plain: A system settings file sets a baseline and takes precedence over other settings, and admin policies override user, workspace and default ones. Enterprise controls are managed through a console. The documentation does not mention lists of allowed or blocked models.
org-policy.technical: The system settings file defines a baseline configuration and acts as overrides, taking precedence over other settings. Admin policies override User, Workspace, and Default policies. Enterprise Admin Controls are customized via the Management Console. The documentation does not mention model allow and deny lists.

outside-tools.plain: It works with MCP servers, which can run as local programs or be reached remotely, and are set up in settings files with optional sign-in. Servers an admin requires are limited to remote connections. Tools can be filtered per server, and admins can list allowed servers.
outside-tools.technical: /mcp manages servers; mcpServers in settings.json (System, Workspace and a third level) or gemini-extension.json. Transports: stdio, SSE, httpUrl (streamable HTTP); admin-required servers support remote transports (sse, http). /mcp OAuth, headers, authProviderType. includeTools and excludeTools; --allowed-mcp-server-names; read-only MCP tools need confirmation in Plan Mode by default.

permission-check.plain: Rules can be set per tool, per path and per shell command, and an older option for pre-allowing tools is deprecated in favour of the policy engine. An LLM-based security checker is off by default and described as an additional layer of protection.
permission-check.technical: --allowed-tools is deprecated in favour of the Policy Engine; tools.core restricts tools; run_shell_command requires manual confirmation; file tools operate within a rootDirectory; run_shell_command(npm test) scopes a command. security.enableConseca (default false) enables an LLM-based checker, an additional layer of protection against unintended actions.

plan-and-ask.plain: Plan mode is a read-only space for designing before implementation, and executing a plan switches to active execution. The footer shows the model name, context usage and the number of loaded instruction files.
plan-and-ask.technical: Plan Mode is read-only; executing a plan switches from plan mode to active execution. Footer shows model name, context usage and number of loaded context files (ui.footer.hideModelInfo hides them). ui.dynamicWindowTitle (default true) shows status icons (Ready, Action Required, Working).

order_note.quote: The policy engine applies the highest-priority rule that matches the tool call.
order_note.text: When several policy rules match a tool call, the highest-priority one is applied.

safety-posture.plain: It has four approval modes: ask each time, auto-approve edits, plan (read-only) and run freely. New folders get a trust check. The documentation disagrees on whether run-freely can be turned on by a keyboard shortcut, and on whether settings merge from two files or four.
safety-posture.technical: --approval-mode: default, auto_edit, yolo, plan; Shift+Tab cycles default, auto_edit, plan. general.defaultApprovalMode defaults to 'default'. --yolo (-y) is deprecated. YOLO is documented as enabled via command line, yet Ctrl+Y toggles it (unreconciled). --skip-trust; /permissions. Two settings.json files vs four merged settings files (unreconciled); policy engine applies the highest-priority matching rule.

send-retry.plain: It routes between models automatically and switches to a fallback model on failure. When the default pro model is rate-limited it switches to flash for the session. The daily limit listed for Google sign-in is 1000 requests.
send-retry.technical: Model routing picks a model and switches to a fallback on model failure (enabled by default); general.plan.modelRouting switches between Pro (planning) and Flash (implementation) by Plan Mode status. Log in with Google: 1000 maximum model requests / user / day. 429 Resource exhausted means the API request limit was exceeded.

shrink-context.plain: The core compresses the conversation automatically before sending it to the model, at a usage level you can set. You can also compress by hand, which swaps the whole chat for a summary. A hook fires before the automatic summary.
shrink-context.technical: model.compressionThreshold sets the fraction of context usage that triggers compression (example values 0.2, 0.3; listed value 0.5). A PreCompress hook fires before the CLI summarizes history. /compress replaces the entire chat context with a summary.

order_note.quote: User and project commands take precedence over extension commands, which have the lowest precedence.
order_note.text: User and project commands take precedence over extension commands, which rank lowest.

skills-commands.plain: A skill is a folder with a description file that the model loads when a task fits. Custom commands are small text files you type yourself, with room for arguments. The documentation does not mention per-skill tool or model overrides, or how commands relate to skills.
skills-commands.technical: Skill: directory with SKILL.md in .gemini/skills (user ~/.gemini/skills/); activate_skill loads it; metadata (~100 words) in context, body (<5k words) after trigger; /skills manages. Custom commands: .toml files in ~/.gemini/commands/; commands/gcs/sync.toml becomes /gcs:sync; {{args}} placeholder. Not mentioned: per-skill tool or model overrides, relation of commands to skills.

subagents.plain: Helpers are defined in text files and can have their own tools and model. The documentation says they cannot call other helpers. It does not mention how many can run at once, in total, or in parallel; separate sessions can use worktrees to avoid collisions.
subagents.technical: Markdown (.md) with YAML frontmatter; name required; tools array (wildcards *, mcp_*, mcp_server_*; omitted inherits parent tools); model defaults to inherit; agents.overrides in settings.json. Subagents cannot call other subagents, even with the * wildcard. Built-in: Codebase Investigator. Not mentioned: concurrency caps, parallel subagents, total agent caps.

surface.plain: You can run it in a terminal, either interactively or headless for scripts. It also documents an IDE connection, an early SDK, and a command that sets up automation to triage issues and review proposed changes.
surface.technical: Run with the gemini command; --prompt-interactive (-i) runs a prompt then continues interactively. Headless: --prompt (-p) forces non-interactive mode; --output-format takes text, json or stream-json. /ide checks IDE integration (VS Code native diffing). v0.30.0 introduced the initial SDK package. /setup-github sets up GitHub Actions to triage issues and review PRs.

thinking.plain: A model setting block can carry reasoning configuration, and the thinking budget can be controlled directly. The entry describes it just as configuration for models with reasoning, without a per-model list of accepted levels.
thinking.technical: generateContentConfig accepts a thinkingConfig object ('Configuration for models with reasoning'); no per-model list of accepted levels is given. Model configuration gives direct control over thinkingBudget alongside temperature. ui.inlineThinkingMode: off or full, default off.

unattended.plain: Shell commands can be moved to the background. Changelog entries mention remote workers and delegating work to remote helpers. The documentation does not mention scheduled routines, remote sessions or event triggers.
unattended.technical: run_shell_command takes an optional is_background argument; /shells toggles the background shells view; tools.shell.backgroundCompletionBehavior controls what happens on completion. Delegation to remote subagents uses Agent-to-Agent. Not mentioned: scheduled routines, remote sessions, event triggers.

undo-point.plain: It can save snapshots automatically for recovery, and you can go back to an earlier state of the conversation. Named checkpoints can be listed, saved, resumed, deleted and shared.
undo-point.technical: /rewind goes back to a previous state in the conversation. Checkpointing automatically saves a snapshot; a setting is described as 'Enable session checkpointing for recovery'. Manual tagged checkpoints support list, save, resume, delete and share subcommands.

updates.plain: It ships on nightly, preview and stable channels, with a weekly cadence promoting code along that path. Release notes are published as a changelog, and deprecations are announced there and in notes inside the docs.
updates.technical: Three channels: nightly, preview, stable; weekly cadence promotes main -> nightly -> preview; nightly runs daily. Stable changelog headed v0.61.0, preview v0.63.0-preview.0. Source checkout: pull latest changes. Release notes at /docs/changelogs. tools.exclude is deprecated in favor of policy rules; the --checkpointing flag was removed.

workspace.plain: It can create an isolated worktree for a run, with a generated name if you give none, but this is documented as needing an experimental setting to be turned on.
workspace.technical: --worktree (-w) creates an isolated worktree and starts Gemini in it; a name is generated if none is given. Requires experimental.worktrees: true in settings. Changelog: 'Added native support for Git worktrees'.

wrap-up.plain: It shows token usage on request and at exit, and records traces through telemetry. A spending setting is scoped to quota exhaustion when AI credits are available: it can prompt each time, use credits automatically, or disable credit usage.
wrap-up.technical: /stats shows token usage and cached token savings. billing.overageStrategy is scoped to quota exhaustion when AI credits are available: ask (prompt each time), always (automatically use credits), never (disable credit usage); default ask. OpenTelemetry (OTel) traces; telemetry includes session.id, installation.id, active_approval_mode. --debug (-d).

assemble-prompt.plain: In a conversation you can paste text, links and images, attach files, and mention Bots or plugins. The desktop composer takes up to six attachments at a time. The documentation does not mention the size of the context window.
assemble-prompt.technical: Paste text, links and images; attach files; reference a saved skill with /; mention a Bot, group, routine or plugin with @. Desktop composer: up to six attachments at a time; documents, images and audio up to 25 MB each, videos up to 200 MB. Context window size: not mentioned in the documentation.

built-in-tools.plain: Its tools are a shell, a browser and computer use on a hosted cloud computer. It runs commands on your own machine only under a local policy that asks for approval by default. The documentation does not mention file editing tools. Sites can block automation or expire a session.
built-in-tools.technical: Shell, browser and computer use run inside the hosted computer. Local commands via the desktop app only under the local execution policy: per-command approval by default, settable to always allow, ask every time, or never; applies to that desktop alone. File read, edit and write tools: not mentioned in the documentation. Web: a site can still block automation or expire a session.

extend-share.plain: Connectors are installed as plugins from a marketplace, and a team admin controls which marketplace plugins members can use; on Teams and Enterprise plans plugins may be required or restricted. The documentation does not mention a packaging format or plugin versioning.
extend-share.technical: Connectors install as plugins from Marketplace; an installed plugin may still need browser authentication. On the Teams plan and the Enterprise plan, team-provided plugins may be required or restricted by an admin. A Cursor team admin controls which marketplace plugins are available. Individual plugin tools can be enabled or disabled. Packaging format and versioning: not mentioned.

order_note.quote: a member's own setting still applies when it is stricter than the team's
order_note.text: A member's own setting still applies when it is stricter than the team's ceiling.

fence.plain: Each user's work runs in a dedicated virtual machine in Cursor's cloud, shared by their Bots. Blocking a plugin leaves that service's website open; closing that needs Network Controls, an Enterprise feature. The documentation does not mention containing commands a Bot starts.
fence.technical: Dedicated Firecracker microVM per user, hardware-level separation; the computer belongs to the account, so anything on it is available to every Bot. Shared workspace: /workspace. Static egress IP addresses; Allow Local Egress is on by default. Blocking a plugin doesn't block the website; closing that takes Network Controls, Enterprise only. Subprocess containment: not mentioned.

hooks.plain: The documentation does not mention hooks: which moments they cover, what kinds of handler they run, how they can block an action, or where they are set up.
hooks.technical: Event catalog, handler types, input contract, output and blocking semantics, matcher semantics, configuration locations, trust and enable controls: the documentation does not mention them.

host-platform.plain: Grok Bot runs on Cursor's cloud computers, uses your Cursor account instead of a separate login, and can delegate coding tasks to Cursor Cloud Agents. On-premises deployment is not supported today. The documentation does not say whether machines are shared with a sibling product.
host-platform.technical: Runs only on Cursor-hosted cloud computers; on-premises and bring-your-own-image deployment not supported today. One dedicated cloud computer per user, shared across that user's Bots; the documentation does not say whether machines or VMs are shared with a sibling product. Shared agent runtime: not mentioned. The one comparison given: the editor's chat and Tab work without the cursorvm.com patterns.

house-rules.plain: Each Bot has a description saying what to work on, which sources to use and when to ask first. Team rules applied to Grok Bot are required, so members must leave them on. The documentation does not mention imports or rules scoped to certain folders.
house-rules.technical: Each Bot has a description (what to work on, which sources, when to ask first); only the Bot's owner can change it. Bots in a group read the group's description. Team Rules apply to every member's Bots, scoped to Cursor, Grok Bot, or both; rules applied to Grok Bot are always required. Import syntax and path-scoped rules: not mentioned in the documentation.

loop.plain: Grok Bot is a computer-use agent that operates apps, browsers and development environments. A direct message takes priority and can redirect the turn; Stop now ends work at once but does not undo actions already done. The documentation does not mention turn or step limits.
loop.technical: Computer-use agent for applications, browsers, and development environments. A direct message takes priority over background work and can redirect the current turn; Stop now ends work immediately, but stopping doesn't undo actions the Bot already completed. Turn and step limits: not mentioned in the documentation.

memory-sessions.plain: A named Bot keeps its memory and preferences between sessions, and chats are stored outside its computer and shared across devices. A copy leaves out history, learned memory and attachments. The documentation does not mention resuming a session. Search may vary during rollout.
memory-sessions.technical: Memory persists per named Bot; Team Bot memory is read by every teammate's conversation. Duplicating a Bot copies profile, settings, enabled skills, routines, avatar, not conversation history, learned memory, or attachments. Chats are stored outside the computer; rm -rf does not delete them. Search: Cmd/Ctrl+K or Cmd/Ctrl+Shift+F; availability can vary during rollout. Resume: not mentioned in the documentation.

model-effort.plain: The vendor says Cursor manages model selection and there is no customer-facing model picker. Usage analytics show which model served each request, and the serving mix can change over time. The documentation does not mention effort levels, bring-your-own-key or a model setting.
model-effort.technical: Cursor manages model selection; no customer-facing model picker, and settings have no model picker. Usage analytics show the model that served each request, including failovers; billing follows the serving model. The serving mix can change over time with no fixed vendor set guaranteed. Model setting and environment, providers and bring-your-own-key, effort values, shared model selection: not mentioned.

org-oversight.plain: Members sign in with their Cursor account through single sign-on, which can be required, and the identity provider can provision users. With Privacy Mode on, customer data is not used for training. Audit logs and user provisioning need the Enterprise plan.
org-oversight.technical: SAML 2.0 SSO with Okta, Microsoft Entra, Google Workspace and OneLogin; can be required for all members. SCIM 2.0 provisioning and deprovisioning: Enterprise only. Privacy Mode: customer data not used for training; Privacy Mode (Legacy) blocks Grok Bot. Audit logs (Enterprise only) cover admin, security and authentication events plus Grok Bot control-plane events.

order_note.quote: members can't turn it off unless a group they belong to lifts the lock with Don't enforce for this group
order_note.text: Enforced Auto-review stays on for members unless a group they belong to lifts the lock.

org-policy.plain: Most settings sit on an admin-only page of the Cursor dashboard, with a few elsewhere. Admins can set team rules, enforce Auto-review and keep a list of allowed models, but several controls need the Enterprise plan, and the model list is not guaranteed to be followed.
org-policy.technical: Most settings: admin-only Grok Bot page of the Cursor dashboard; a few in Team Settings, Team Marketplace or the identity provider. Team Setup (managed setup, via manifests) is Enterprise only, as is enforcing Auto-review. Team admins set Team Rules, Cloud Agent delegation, template sharing, local execution ceiling. Model allowlist: Enterprise only; enforcement is not guaranteed.

outside-tools.plain: Outside services connect as plugins, via MCP calls that Cursor runs. You log in through your browser, and tokens stay on Cursor's side. The team's connector policy applies; its allowlist needs the Enterprise plan, and pushing connectors to members is not available.
outside-tools.technical: Hosted connector calls are MCP calls Cursor runs. A Command server runs on whichever computer the conversation uses; custom servers needing secrets: choose Remote HTTPS. Connectors appear as plugins,; pushing connectors to members, mandatory or default-on, is not available. MCP allowlist: Enterprise only. Blocking a plugin doesn't block the website; closing that takes Network Controls (Enterprise only).

order_note.quote: Ask first rules always stop matching actions
order_note.text: Ask-first rules stop matching actions; allow rules let them proceed only if the reviewer finds no other reason to stop.

permission-check.plain: Members can add Auto-review rules: ask-first rules stop matching actions, allow rules proceed only if the reviewer finds no other reason. A review model checks risky actions, but is skipped where nobody can answer an approval card unless an Enterprise admin enforces it.
permission-check.technical: Auto-review rules (Settings > General > Auto-review): Ask first rules always stop matching actions; Allow automatically rules proceed only when the reviewer finds no other reason to stop. Example: Allow automatically when running git status in /workspace/reports. Auto Review covers shell commands, plugin calls, computer use, automation writes, delegation; described as applying 'With enforcement on'.

plan-and-ask.plain: The sidebar marks Bots that need attention, have unread activity or are working, and notifications can tell you when a Bot finishes or needs input. The documentation does not mention a plan mode.
plan-and-ask.technical: Sidebar distinguishes Bots that need attention (a question, approval, or handoff), unread activity (a new result), and working status. Notifications in a Bot's settings give a system or mobile notification when it finishes or needs input. Plan mode: not mentioned in the documentation.

order_note.quote: Ask first wins if two rules conflict
order_note.text: If two Auto-review rules conflict, the one that says to ask first wins.

safety-posture.plain: Prompts offer allow once, always allow or deny; commands on your own computer default to per-command approval, set per desktop. Team admins can cap this; it is separate from cloud approvals. The documentation does not mention named, auto-accept or read-only modes.
safety-posture.technical: Approval prompts: Allow once, Always allow, Deny. Local execution: per-command approval by default, applies to that desktop alone; a team admin can cap it; separate from the approvals for work on the cloud computer. Local-access default: Ask every time; default mode and whether a choice persists not stated. Team Auto-review rules: Enterprise only. Named modes, auto-accept, read-only: not mentioned.

send-retry.plain: Cursor picks the model for each task, and the mix of serving models can change over time. Paid access includes weekly usage; when it runs out, extra usage continues as on-demand usage if that is turned on, and otherwise Grok Bot stops and says the limit was reached.
send-retry.technical: Cursor picks the model for the specific task; the serving model mix can change over time with no fixed vendor set guaranteed; usage analytics show the serving model, including failovers. Paid Grok Bot access includes Weekly usage, which resets weekly. If on-demand is enabled, On-demand usage continues after it runs out; if off, Grok Bot stops and the screen says you have reached your Grok Bot usage limit.

shrink-context.plain: The documentation does not mention automatic or manual compaction of a long conversation.
shrink-context.technical: Automatic compaction and manual compaction: the documentation does not mention them.

skills-commands.plain: A skill is a set of reusable instructions, and a demonstration can become a draft skill. Type a slash in the composer to pick one; a private skill missing from the menu must be switched on for that Bot. The documentation does not mention custom or built-in commands.
skills-commands.technical: Skill: steps, decision rules, expected output, safety boundaries; Teach a task turns a demonstration into a draft. Type / to reference a skill; @ mentions a Bot, group, routine or plugin. A private skill missing from the / menu: enable it under Settings > Plugins > Yours; a Bot may still need the relevant plugin or login. Not mentioned: resource loading, skill overrides, built-in or custom commands, arguments.

subagents.plain: A Bot has a name, label and description set by its owner, and Bots can create helper Bots. Bots run in parallel, each with its own screen and one computer-use task at a time; a group chat takes two to six Bots. The documentation does not mention tool lists or built-in types.
subagents.technical: Bot: name, label, description. Bots can suggest or create a helper Bot. Each Bot gets its own screen: one computer-use task per screen at a time; one bulk computer operation per team at a time. Group chat: select two to six Bots; a teammate's published Team Bot can join, but not alongside Bots that run on your own computer. Tool allow-list, per-agent model and effort, built-in types: not mentioned.

surface.plain: It is reached through desktop and phone apps, a script-driven Organization API, and Slack for Team Bots. The documentation does not mention a terminal, headless or editor route. The script route needs an admin-level key, and Slack needs a published Bot added by its owner.
surface.technical: Desktop app: macOS (Apple silicon and Intel), Windows (x64 and Arm64), Linux (x64 and Arm64); phone app: iPhone and Android. Organization API: send a team, members and an action, then poll; needs an Organization API key with admin:* scope. Slack: owner adds a published Team Bot; each teammate links their Slack account first. Interactive CLI, headless mode, IDE integration: not mentioned in the documentation.

thinking.plain: The documentation does not mention how thinking effort depends on the model, or whether the reasoning budget is shown or hidden.
thinking.technical: Model dependence, and thinking budget and visibility: the documentation does not mention them.

unattended.plain: Bots work on a persistent cloud computer, so work continues while your laptop is closed, and routines can run on a schedule or when something happens, such as a Slack message. Approvals for work you did not start expire after about 10 minutes. Admins can disable delegation.
unattended.technical: Persistent cloud computer with browser, filesystem and terminal; work continues while the laptop is closed. Approvals from work that started without you, like a routine or a message from another Bot, expire after about 10 minutes. Routines run on a schedule or on events (Slack, GitHub, Linear, Sentry, PagerDuty, email, webhook). Admins can disable spawning; on-premises deployment is not supported today.

undo-point.plain: The documentation describes a reset that rebuilds the computer from your last saved snapshot.
undo-point.technical: Reset rebuilds the computer from your last saved snapshot.

updates.plain: The desktop app checks for updates itself, and the account menu shows the version and offers to install and restart. Changes are listed on the Cursor changelog. The vendor does not publish how long older installers stay available, and an unsupported build must update.
updates.technical: About shows Version; Copy version info copies version, release track, and OS. Feed per platform: https://api2.cursor.sh/updates/api/download/stable/{platform}/sand. Changelog: https://cursor.com/changelog. Grok Bot requires an update when a version is more than 14 days old and a newer version is out. Cursor doesn't publish how long older installers stay available; a pinned build works only until support stops.

workspace.plain: The documentation does not mention a way to give the agent its own isolated copy of a project, such as a worktree.
workspace.technical: Worktree isolation: the documentation does not mention it.

wrap-up.plain: Usage and billing screens show weekly and on-demand usage, and a monthly on-demand cap can be set, but a running task can go a little past it. Action recording and a telemetry export to a collector are offered, the export on the Enterprise plan; recording is off by default.
wrap-up.technical: Usage & Billing shows weekly included and on-demand usage. On-demand cap: Settings > On-demand monthly limit; a separate Grok Bot spend cap is not available today; the cap does not stop a Bot in the middle of a run. OpenTelemetry Export (Team Settings): Enterprise only. Action Recording: off by default, 90 day retention, not on the Audit Log page.

assemble-prompt.plain: A context window setting gives the size in tokens and drives when automatic compaction happens. Rule files are loaded in full with no size cap. One option adds text to the system prompt for a run, and another replaces it entirely.
assemble-prompt.technical: context_window gives the size in tokens and drives auto-compact timing. A prompt can reference a file as @src/main.rs. [tools] respect_gitignore (default false) skips gitignored files in search and read tools. Rule files load in full, with no size cap. --rules appends text to the system prompt for a single run; --system-prompt-override replaces it entirely.

built-in-tools.plain: Built-in tools can be allowed or removed by name. Shell commands time out after 120 seconds by default, and long-running ones run as background tasks. The web fetch tool is off by default for security, and the write tool can be switched off for read-only sessions.
built-in-tools.technical: --tools <LIST> and --disallowed-tools <LIST>; [features] lsp_tools (default off). [toolset.bash] timeout_secs default 120; x kills a selected background task; ! is shell mode. [toolset] file_toolset standard (default) or hashline; [features] write_file (default on); GROK_WRITE_FILE 0 disables write. GROK_WEB_FETCH (1/0, off by default); [toolset.web_fetch] allowed_domains; --disable-web-search.

extend-share.plain: Plugins can add skills, agents, hooks, MCP servers and language servers, and marketplace sources are listed in settings, with a marketplace tab for browsing and installing. Claude Code plugins are read too. The documentation does not mention a packaging format or versioning.
extend-share.technical: Plugins add skills, agents, hooks, MCP servers and LSP servers. Sources: [[marketplace.sources]] in ~/.grok/config.toml and ~/.grok/plugins/known_marketplaces.json; a paths list under [skills]/[plugins]; the TUI has a Marketplace tab. [plugins] enabled takes name lists (project plugins may default off). The documentation does not mention packaging format or versioning and update.

fence.plain: The sandbox is off by default; once on, it limits what the agent and its child processes can read, write and reach. Built-in profiles do not permanently protect paths like the SSH folder, and the network limits on child processes are enforced on Linux.
fence.technical: Landlock on Linux, Seatbelt on macOS; [sandbox] profile, --sandbox or GROK_SANDBOX. Profiles: off (default), workspace, read-only, strict or custom. restrict_network (Linux seccomp): no-op on macOS for read-only / strict; model API and web tools are not blocked. Built-ins do not permanently protect ~/.ssh. The documentation does not mention a sandbox override.

hooks.plain: Hooks run a command, or send the event to a web address, at tool and session events. The hook that runs before a tool is the one that can block it; timeouts, crashes and malformed output let the tool call go ahead. Project hooks need trust before they run.
hooks.technical: type is "command" or "http" (url to POST to); timeout in seconds, default 5. PreToolUse is the blocking event; also Stop, StopFailure, SubagentStart, SubagentStop. Exit 0 allows, exit 2 denies; timeouts, crashes and malformed output are fail-open. matcher is a regular expression on the tool name. ~/.grok/hooks/*.json, <project>/.grok/hooks/*.json. /hooks-trust or --trust.

host-platform.plain: The documentation does not mention a host platform, a shared account and billing, shared servers or agent runtime, delegation to another agent, or distinct harness features.
host-platform.technical: The documentation does not mention host platform, shared account and billing, shared execution infrastructure, shared agent runtime, delegates to, or distinct harness features.

order_note.quote: deeper files take precedence on conflicts
order_note.text: When rule files conflict, the file deeper in the folder tree takes precedence.

house-rules.plain: It reads instruction files and rule folders in a project, including Claude Code ones, and skips files that git ignores. Deeper files win on a conflict, and a nested file covers its own folder tree. The documentation does not mention an import syntax.
house-rules.technical: Per directory: AGENTS.md, Agents.md, AGENT.md, CLAUDE.md, Claude.md, CLAUDE.local.md and the *.md files in .grok/rules/ (.claude/rules/, .cursor/rules/ read for compatibility); gitignored files are skipped. Deeper files take precedence on conflicts; a nested AGENTS.md scopes to its subtree. --rules adds rules for a single run. The documentation does not mention an import syntax.

loop.plain: You can cap the number of agent turns, and shell commands have their own timeout. The documentation does not mention the loop's shape.
loop.technical: --max-turns <N> sets the maximum number of agent turns; [toolset.bash] timeout_secs sets the foreground bash command timeout (seconds, default 120). The documentation does not mention the loop shape.

memory-sessions.plain: Cross-session memory is off by default, and its commands appear once it is switched on. Conversations are saved on disk, keyed by working directory, and can be resumed, forked, listed, renamed and exported, with the same sessions in the terminal, headless and editor use.
memory-sessions.technical: [memory] enabled is the master switch (default off); --experimental-memory; /remember <note>; grok memory clear [--workspace|--global|--all]. -r, --resume [<ID>]; -c, --continue; /resume; /fork [directive]; --fork-session. Sessions are saved under ~/.grok/sessions/, keyed by working directory; grok export <session-id> [output]; grok sessions <list|search|delete>; /rename <title>.

order_note.quote: model.api_key > model.env_key > active session token > XAI_API_KEY
order_note.text: A model's own key is used first, then its environment variable, then the active session token, then the general xAI key.

model-effort.plain: You can pick a model from a picker, a command, a startup option or a default setting, and add your own keyed models. Effort levels are given for Grok 4.7, and the documentation does not state a default value. It does not mention shared model selection.
model-effort.technical: Ctrl+M picker; /model <name> (alias /m); -m, --model <MODEL>; GROK_DEFAULT_MODEL; [models] hidden_models. [model.<id>] defines custom/BYOK models. grok-4.7 is on the xAI API. Grok 4.7 supports low, medium, high and xhigh; [models] default_reasoning_effort; /effort. The documentation does not state a default value or mention shared model selection.

org-oversight.plain: It supports sign-in through a corporate identity provider and device-code login for headless use. Zero data retention is set per team, with session history kept locally. The documentation does not mention admin audit reports.
org-oversight.technical: Four session authentication methods; corporate identity provider (Entra ID, Okta, Auth0); grok login --device-auth; force_login_team_uuid pins login to a team. ZDR is enforced at the team level; local session history is stored in ~/.grok/; /privacy shows or toggles status. Under ZDR, video tools return an error until user-supplied storage is configured. The documentation does not mention admin audit and reporting.

order_note.quote: wins over hidden
order_note.text: A model on the disabled list is removed from the catalog, and that wins over merely hiding it.

org-policy.plain: An administrator can push settings files onto machines, switch off the mode that skips permission prompts, and limit which models can be picked. A lock is honored from root-owned locations, not from a file the user can edit.
org-policy.technical: Managed scope reads ~/.grok/managed_config.toml or /etc/grok/managed_config.toml; /etc/grok/requirements.toml is recommended for MDM; grok setup fetches managed configuration. disable_bypass_permissions_mode = true under [ui] turns always-approve off, honored from root-owned sources, not the user-writable ~/.grok/requirements.toml. [models] allowed_models, disabled_models.

order_note.quote: merged below config.toml in priority
order_note.text: Settings read from the Claude Code, Cursor and project config files are merged in below the main Grok settings file in priority.

outside-tools.plain: It connects MCP servers whose tools appear next to the built-in ones. Servers are set up in user or project settings, and Claude Code and Cursor configs are read too. A project server replaces a user one with the same name. Trusting a project also covers its MCP servers.
outside-tools.technical: Tools are namespaced <server>__<tool>; grok mcp <list|add|remove|doctor>. url in [mcp_servers.<name>] is an HTTP/SSE MCP server. Declared in ~/.grok/config.toml or project .grok/config.toml (a same-name project server replaces the user one); ~/.claude.json, .cursor/mcp.json and .mcp.json merge below config.toml. bearer_token_env_var; --header is repeatable. GROK_TOOL_SEARCH (1/0). /hooks-trust or --trust.

order_note.quote: `deny` always wins over `allow`
order_note.text: A deny rule wins over an allow rule.

permission-check.plain: Rules can allow, deny or ask by tool, by path pattern or by shell command pattern, and a deny rule beats an allow rule. Auto mode uses a classifier to auto-approve safe tools; dangerous ones may still prompt, and it is toggled when the feature is enabled.
permission-check.technical: --allow / --deny filters include Bash, Edit, Read, MCPTool, WebFetch and WebSearch; [permission] allow / deny / ask hold rules like Bash(git *), Edit(**/*.rs). A remembered always allow grant still prompts for rm and git push; an explicit config or CLI allow rule auto-approves them. Auto: auto-approves safe tools, dangerous ones may still prompt; toggled with /auto or Shift+Tab when the feature is enabled.

plan-and-ask.plain: In plan mode just the plan file can be edited until you approve, and plan review is not skipped under auto or the skip-prompts mode. It gates edit tools, not the shell, so commands can still write through redirection. A bottom row shows live values such as context use and cost.
plan-and-ask.technical: Plan mode: the session plan file can be edited until approval, independent of permission mode; leave with Shift+Tab when idle or q on the approval screen. Gates edit tools, not the shell: bash can still write via redirection. status_line default is disabled; the context item turns amber at the auto-compaction threshold or 80 percent; cost is hidden below $0.005.

order_note.quote: permission_mode wins when more than one is set
order_note.text: If an older setting and the newer permission mode setting are both set, the newer one wins.

safety-posture.plain: It asks before running anything not already allowed. Modes include plan, auto and one that skips permission prompts. The default mode comes from user or managed settings, not project ones. For read-only sessions it describes switching off the write tool, not a named mode.
safety-posture.technical: Ask is the default; [ui] permission_mode takes default, ask, auto or always-approve; dontAsk silently denies without an allow rule. Shift+Tab cycles Normal, Plan, Auto (when available) and Always-approve; --always-approve (alias --yolo). Order is deny > ask > allow. Default mode: user config or managed/requirements, not project .grok/config.toml. GROK_WRITE_FILE 0 disables the write tool.

send-retry.plain: The documentation does not mention automatic model routing, or how it behaves when it is rate-limited or the service is busy.
send-retry.technical: The documentation does not mention automatic routing or rate-limit behaviour.

shrink-context.plain: It compacts the conversation automatically as the context window fills, at a set percent of usage, and you can compact by hand with optional notes on what to keep. Hooks can run before and after compaction.
shrink-context.technical: [session] auto_compact_threshold_percent (0–100, default 85); PreCompact and PostCompact events; the context status item turns amber at the auto-compaction threshold, or at 80 percent when the agent reports none. /compact [context] compresses the history, with optional instructions about what to preserve.

skills-commands.plain: Skills are reusable instruction folders that also appear as slash commands. The vendor says a skill's tool list does not grant or restrict tools and model settings are not applied. The documentation gives an autocomplete hint for arguments but not how they are passed.
skills-commands.technical: SKILL.md has YAML frontmatter, extra keys ignored; found in ./.grok/skills/ and [skills] paths. /<skill-name>; /local:commit on a collision; disable-model-invocation (default false); user-invocable (default true). allowed-tools does not grant or restrict tools; model, effort, license, compatibility are not applied. argument-hint is an autocomplete hint. The documentation does not mention resource loading.

subagents.plain: Helpers include a read-only explorer and a planner, can get their own model, and run as parallel child sessions. The documentation does not settle whether subagents are on out of the box, and the one cap it states is for scheduled tasks. It does not mention nesting.
subagents.technical: Built-in explore (read, list, search; no shell, no edits) and plan; types under .grok/agents/ or ~/.grok/agents/; [subagents.models]. GROK_SUBAGENTS defaults to 0 while Workflows are on by default; unsettled out of the box. At most 50 scheduled tasks; no limit stated on concurrent agents. The documentation does not mention nesting rules, per-agent effort or total agent caps.

surface.plain: Running it in a terminal opens a full-screen interface, and it can also run inline. It can run in scripts without a screen and connect to editors through the Agent Client Protocol. The documentation does not mention desktop or web apps, or build-pipeline and chat services.
surface.technical: Plain grok starts the interactive TUI; [ui] screen_mode is fullscreen (default when unset) or minimal; --no-alt-screen runs inline. Headless: --output-format plain, json or streaming-json; set XAI_API_KEY for CI/CD. grok agent stdio runs an ACP agent over JSON-RPC on stdin/stdout. The documentation does not mention desktop or web apps or CI and chat surfaces.

thinking.plain: Reasoning controls apply when the chosen model supports them, and levels are listed for Grok 4.7. The documentation covers showing or hiding thinking blocks and the width of the thoughts panel, but does not state a token budget.
thinking.technical: Per-model supports_reasoning_effort / reasoning_effort apply when supported; Grok 4.7 supports low, medium, high and xhigh. GROK_SHOW_THINKING_BLOCKS (default 1); [ui] show_thinking_blocks (default true); [ui] max_thoughts_width (40-500, default 120). The documentation does not state a token budget.

unattended.plain: Commands, subagents and monitors can run in the background, and a recurring loop re-runs a prompt but expires after 7 days, with 50 scheduled tasks at most. A monitor turns each line a script prints into a notification. The documentation does not mention remote sessions.
unattended.technical: Ctrl+B backgrounds a command; /tasks; [toolset.bash] auto_background_on_timeout (default true). /loop [interval] <prompt>: Ns (minimum 60), Nm, Nh, Nd; loops expire after 7 days; at most 50 scheduled tasks. Grok Bot (/grok-bot/overview) is described as "AI teammates on a cloud computer". The documentation does not mention remote sessions or delegation to other agents.

undo-point.plain: A rewind command lists a rewind point per prompt, and picking one restores the files and trims the conversation to match. Rewinding changes files on disk, so reverted changes are lost unless they were committed to git.
undo-point.technical: /rewind (or Esc Esc while idle) lists a rewind point per prompt; selecting one restores files to their state at that point and truncates the conversation to match. Rewind modifies files on disk; reverted changes are lost unless committed to git.

updates.plain: It has stable and alpha release channels, an update command, and ways to switch off background update checks. A command shows release notes for the current version. The documentation does not mention a deprecation policy or the version it covers.
updates.technical: [cli] channel is stable or alpha; grok update accepts --alpha and --stable, checks for updates or installs a specific version. Background checks: --no-auto-update, auto_update = false under [cli] in ~/.grok/config.toml, or GROK_DISABLE_AUTOUPDATER. /release-notes (alias /changelog) views release notes for the current version. The documentation does not mention a deprecation policy.

workspace.plain: A worktree session runs in its own copy of your repository so parallel agents do not overwrite each other's files. It needs a git repository and starts from your current state, including uncommitted changes.
workspace.technical: -w, --worktree [<NAME>] starts the session in a new git worktree; worktrees require a git repository, live under ~/.grok/worktrees/<repo>/<name> and start from your current HEAD, including uncommitted changes.

wrap-up.plain: You can view credit usage, a running cost in the status line, and log files for debugging. Policies such as disabling telemetry can be set in a requirements file. The documentation does not mention budgets or spending caps.
wrap-up.technical: /usage views credit usage; status line cost item (hidden below $0.005); /context or /session-info. /etc/grok/requirements.toml is authoritative for compliance-critical policies such as disabling telemetry. GROK_LOG_FILE; --debug; GROK_CRASH_HANDLER (default 0). The documentation does not mention budgets and caps.
